title: Median of Two Sorted Arrays
description: Brute force to optimized: merging both arrays and reading the middle versus a binary search for a valid partition point, reading the median off just 4 boundary values.

blocks.text: Problem Summary: Given two sorted arrays nums1 and nums2, of sizes m and n, return the median of the two arrays combined, in O(log(m plus n)) time.

blocks.caption: What goes in, what comes out

blocks.text: Find the value that would sit in the middle if nums1 and nums2 were merged into one sorted sequence (or the average of the two middle values, if the combined length is even), without necessarily building that merged sequence.

blocks.title: Analogy: Splitting Two Sorted Card Piles Into Matching Halves
blocks.text: Picture two separately sorted piles of numbered cards, and needing to slide a divider through EACH pile so that all the cards to the left of both dividers, combined, form exactly the smaller (or equal) half of the combined deck, and everything on the left is still no larger than anything on the right.

blocks.caption: Split both arrays so the combined left portion is exactly half; the median follows directly

blocks.text: Merged, the sequence is [1,2,3], an odd total length of 3; the median is the middle value, 2.0.
Merged, the sequence is [1,2,3,4], an even total length of 4; the median is the average of the two middle values, 2.5.
Before merging both arrays fully, notice the median can be found purely by locating the right SPLIT POINT in each array, without ever combining or sorting anything.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: If a partition point i in nums1 and a partition point j in nums2 are chosen so that i plus j equals exactly half (rounded appropriately) of the combined length, then the combined "left of both partitions" and "right of both partitions" groups have the correct sizes for computing the median.

Observation 2: That partition is VALID exactly when the largest value on the left side of nums1 is no greater than the smallest value on the right side of nums2, and vice versa, ensuring every left-side value is truly no larger than every right-side value.

Observation 3: As the partition point in nums1 increases, its left side's maximum value only grows, and nums2's corresponding partition point (determined by the size constraint) shifts left, giving a monotonic relationship binary search can exploit.

Observation 4: Binary searching on the smaller array's partition point, adjusting based on which side of the validity condition fails, converges on the correct partition in logarithmic time.

This leads to binary searching for the correct partition point in the smaller array, deriving the other array's partition point from the size constraint, and reading the median directly off the four boundary values once a valid partition is found.
Merge both arrays into one combined sorted array, then read off the middle value or values directly.

items: Merge nums1 and nums2 into a single array.
Sort the merged array (or merge them while already sorted, in linear time).
If the combined length is odd, return the middle element; if even, return the average of the two middle elements.

blocks.caption: Brute force flow: merge, then read off the middle value(s) directly

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Both arrays are combined into one list and sorted from scratch, ignoring that each was already individually sorted.
The median is read off directly once the combined array is fully in order.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O((m plus n) log(m plus n)), dominated by the sort (O(m plus n) if merging the already-sorted arrays directly instead of re-sorting).
Space: O(m plus n) for the merged array.
Limitation: the problem explicitly asks for O(log(m plus n)) time, which a full merge, even an efficient linear one, cannot achieve; a fundamentally different, partition-based approach is needed.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why merging is too slow: any approach that looks at every element takes at least linear time, but the target complexity is logarithmic in the combined size.

What replaces merging: partitioning both arrays directly, choosing split points that guarantee the correct number of elements on each side, without ever combining values.

How to find the right partition quickly: binary search on the partition point of the SMALLER array (to keep the search space small), deriving the other array's partition point from the required total size on the left, and adjusting based on whether the boundary values satisfy the validity condition.

The core idea: binary search directly for the partition, and once valid, compute the median from just the four boundary values around it, with no merging at all.

Always binary search on the smaller of the two arrays. For a candidate partition i in nums1, compute j in nums2 so the left side across both arrays has exactly half (rounded up) of the total elements. Check whether nums1's left-side max is at most nums2's right-side min, and nums2's left-side max is at most nums1's right-side min; if not, shift the binary search based on which comparison failed. Once valid, compute the median directly from the four boundary values.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Partition i in nums1","Partition j in nums2","Left1/Right1, Left2/Right2","Valid?"],"rows":[["1 (left=[1], right=[3])","1 (left=[2], right=[])","Left1=1<=Right2=inf, Left2=2<=Right1=3","yes; median = max(1,2) = 2 (odd total)"]]}

blocks.caption: Optimized flow: binary search the partition, read the median off just 4 boundary values

blocks.text: Fixing i plus j to exactly half the combined size guarantees that, once a valid partition is found, the left side across both arrays holds exactly the correct count of the smallest elements, and the right side holds the rest, without ever needing to merge or sort. The validity check, each array's left-side maximum not exceeding the other array's right-side minimum, confirms every left value is truly no greater than every right value, letting the median be read directly from the four boundary values.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(log(min(m, n))), binary searching only the smaller array.
Space: O(1).

blocks.text: This is one of the most well-known "binary search on the answer's structure, not on a single array" problems: instead of searching for a value, the search is for a valid PARTITION point, and the median is read directly from the boundary values once that partition is found.

items: Binary searching the larger array instead of the smaller one, which can push the partition point in the other array out of valid bounds.
Forgetting to handle empty-side boundaries (partition at 0 or at the array's length) with positive/negative infinity sentinels.
Mixing up which array's comparison failing means "shrink" versus "grow" the partition.

blocks.text: Framing the problem as "find a partition, not a value" up front, and explaining the validity condition (left maxes no greater than the opposite right mins) clearly, demonstrates the core insight before any code is written.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text:
If the interviewer says "the required time is logarithmic, not linear", think: binary search a partition point, not a merge.
If the interviewer says "why search the smaller array", think: it keeps the binary search range small and guarantees the other array's partition point stays in valid bounds.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: The brute force runs in O((m+n) log(m+n)) time and O(m+n) space. The optimized partition-based binary search runs in O(log(min(m,n))) time and O(1) space.

items: Pattern: binary search for a valid partition point across two sorted arrays.

Core Idea: choose partitions in both arrays summing to exactly half the combined size, and binary search until every left-side value is no greater than every right-side value; the median follows directly from the boundary values.
Time: O((m+n) log(m+n)) for the brute force, O(log(min(m,n))) for the optimized partition search.
Space: O(m+n) for the brute force, O(1) for the optimized approach.
Most Important Observation: the median can be found from a valid partition's boundary values alone, with no merging required.
Interview Difficulty: a classic hard problem; the partition validity condition and infinity sentinels are the trickiest details to get exactly right.
One line memory trick: binary search the smaller array's partition; the median lives at its boundary.
